title: Let's Learn English
author: VOA Learning English
description: A short, real beginner conversation for practicing greetings, names, and spelling.
levelReason: Short sentences, everyday greetings, clear turn-taking, and repeated names
learningGoal: Introduce yourself, greet someone, and spell a name in a short conversation.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Hi! Are you Anna?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes! Hi there! Are you Pete?

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: I am Pete.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Nice to meet you.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Let's try that again. I'm Anna. Nice to meet you.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: I'm Pete. Anna — is that A-N-A?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: No. A-N-N-A.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Well, Anna with two n's — welcome!

vocabulary.meaning: A friendly, informal way to say hello.
vocabulary.example: Hi there! Are you new here?

vocabulary.meaning: A polite phrase used when meeting someone for the first time.
vocabulary.example: I am Mia. Nice to meet you.

vocabulary.meaning: Do something one more time.
vocabulary.example: Let's try again more slowly.

vocabulary.meaning: To greet someone kindly when they arrive.
vocabulary.example: We welcome new students to the class.

questions.prompt: Who is new to the building?
How many letter N’s are in Anna’s name?
Which phrase do they use when they first meet?

title: Let's Learn English
author: VOA Learning English
description: Anna meets a neighbour in the hallway of her new building. Names, apartment numbers and where you are from, in fifteen short turns.
levelReason: Three speakers, but they take strict turns and almost every sentence is four to eight words. The only thing to hold in your head is which apartment belongs to whom
learningGoal: Say where you are from, give your apartment number, and greet a neighbour you have just met.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Hey, Pete! Who’s your friend?

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: She is Anna. She is new to D.C.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Where are you from?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I am from a small town.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Well, welcome to D.C.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: I am Jonathan. I am in apartment B4.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I am in apartment C2. Marsha is my roommate.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: I know Marsha. She is nice.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: And I am in Apartment D7. I have to go now.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh!

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Remember to call Marsha at work. Tell her you’re here.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Right, thanks, Pete. Nice to meet you!

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: You too, Bye.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Apartment C2, here I come!

vocabulary.meaning: Asks what place someone comes from — a town, a city or a country. The answer is usually just the place: “I am from a small town.”
vocabulary.example: Where are you from? I am from a small town.

vocabulary.meaning: Said to someone arriving somewhere for the first time, with the place after it.
vocabulary.example: Well, welcome to D.C.

vocabulary.meaning: A person you share an apartment with. Not a neighbour — a roommate is inside the same apartment.
vocabulary.example: Marsha is my roommate.

vocabulary.meaning: Must leave now. The polite way to end a conversation before it finishes on its own.
vocabulary.example: I have to go now.

questions.prompt: Which apartment does Anna live in?
What does Pete tell Anna to do?

title: Let's Learn English
author: VOA Learning English
description: Anna cannot find a pen in her bag and pulls out everything else instead. A running joke that repeats “I have a…” until the name of each object sticks.
levelReason: ≈110 wpm and nearly a fifth of the running time is silence. The sentence frame never changes — “I have a…”, “It is a…” — so each new turn changes exactly one word, and that word is always a concrete object you can picture
learningGoal: Ask whether somebody has something, say what you have, and name everyday objects with “It is a…”.

vocabulary.meaning: The ordinary way to ask if someone is carrying something. “Do you have” + the thing, with no extra words in between.
vocabulary.example: Anna, do you have a pen?

vocabulary.meaning: Tacked onto the end of a sentence to push back gently on what was just said — close to “but still”. Very common in speech, almost never at the start.
vocabulary.example: I know I have a pen, though…

vocabulary.meaning: Asks the reason someone is carrying or keeping something. Not a complaint — usually just surprise.
vocabulary.example: Why do you have a map of the world?

vocabulary.meaning: An invitation to go out together. “Get coffee” means the outing, not the drink.
vocabulary.example: I have a pen! Let’s get coffee!

title: Let's Learn English
author: VOA Learning English
description: Marsha shows Anna around a house one room at a time. Each room is named, then paired with the thing you do in it.
levelReason: ≈97 wpm with 37% of the running time silent — the most room to think of anything in the catalogue. Two speakers, and every line repeats the room name the line before it introduced
learningGoal: Name the rooms of a house and say what happens in each one: cook in the kitchen, relax in the living room, sleep in the bedroom.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hello, everyone! Today my friend Marsha is at her friend's house. She says it is beautiful. I want to see this house! Here we are!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Marsha, I am in the kitchen! It is a beautiful kitchen!

transcript.speaker: Marsha
transcript.text: It is beautiful. We cook in the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I eat in the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: Marsha
transcript.text: We relax in the living room.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I relax in the living room. Marsha, let’s go upstairs!

transcript.speaker: Marsha
transcript.text: Anna? Where are you?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Marsha, I am in the bathroom! I wash in the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: Marsha
transcript.text: I am in the bedroom. We sleep in the bedroom.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I sleep in the bedroom!

vocabulary.meaning: Asked when you cannot see the person you are talking to. The answer is “I am in the…” plus a room.
vocabulary.example: Anna? Where are you?

vocabulary.meaning: The room a household sits in together. Two words, and neither one is “sitting”.
vocabulary.example: We relax in the living room.

vocabulary.meaning: To rest and do nothing in particular. Used of people, not of things.
vocabulary.example: I relax in the living room.

vocabulary.meaning: On or to the floor above. It is already a direction, so it takes no preposition: “go upstairs”, never “go to upstairs”.
vocabulary.example: Marsha, let’s go upstairs!

questions.prompt: What does Marsha say they do in the kitchen?
What does Anna do in the bathroom?
Whose house are they looking at?

title: Let's Learn English
author: VOA Learning English
description: Anna wants the gym and keeps finding the mailroom. The same directions come back four times, and each time one more preposition of place has to land.
levelReason: Joint slowest in the catalogue at ≈83 wpm, tied with Lesson 1 over three times the length. What lifts it above the other beginner lessons is not the speed but what has to be tracked: across from, next to and behind all point at rooms you cannot see, and the joke only works if you hear that Anna is getting them wrong
learningGoal: Ask where a room is, and understand the answer when it is given as a relation to another room — across from, next to, behind.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hi there! I’m Anna and I live in Washington, D.C. Every day I learn more about this great city. People in Washington like to work out! Oh, hi, Pete. How’s it going?

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Hi, Anna. It’s going great. How’s it going with you?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Things are awesome! Pete, I want to work out. Where is the gym?

transcript.speaker: Pete

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Thanks, Pete!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh, Pete. This is not the gym.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: That’s right, Anna. This is the mailroom.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: The gym is across from … what?

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: The gym is across from the lounge.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Across from the lounge. Right. Thanks!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Pete! This is not the gym!

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: The gym is across from the lounge. It is behind the lobby.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Right. Right. See you.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: See you, Anna!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: See you.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: See you, Anna.

transcript.speaker: Pete

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I’m good.

vocabulary.meaning: To exercise, usually at a gym. Nothing to do with solving a problem, which is the other meaning of the same two words.
vocabulary.example: Pete, I want to work out.

vocabulary.meaning: On the opposite side of a corridor or street, facing it. Two words in American English; British English says “opposite”.
vocabulary.example: The gym is across from the lounge.

vocabulary.meaning: Immediately beside, sharing a wall. Closer than “near”.
vocabulary.example: It’s next to the mailroom.

vocabulary.meaning: On the far side of, hidden by. Used here of a room you reach by going past another one.
vocabulary.example: It is behind the lobby.

vocabulary.meaning: A casual “how are you?”. The expected reply is another set phrase — “It’s going great” — not an actual report.
vocabulary.example: Oh, hi, Pete. How’s it going?

title: Let's Learn English
author: VOA Learning English
episode: Lesson 10: Come Over to My Place
description: Ashley is coming over and cannot find the building. Anna gives directions from the Metro, then has to add a landmark when the first set turns out not to be enough.
levelReason: ≈97 wpm, and it is a phone call — no face to read, and the directions arrive as a list: exit, turn right, turn left, straight ahead. Ashley repeats each step back, which is the lesson's own admission that four instructions at once is the hard part
learningGoal: Give and confirm directions on the phone — exit, turn right, straight ahead — and fall back on a landmark when the address is not enough.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hi! Today, my friend Ashley, is coming over. I am showing her my new apartment! Oh! That’s Ashley calling.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hi Ashley!

transcript.speaker: Ashley

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hi, Ashley.

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Ashley
transcript.text: Okay. See you soon.

transcript.speaker: Anna

vocabulary.meaning: To visit somebody at their home. “Over” carries the whole idea of crossing town to get there.
vocabulary.example: Today, my friend Ashley is coming over.

vocabulary.meaning: To leave a building or a station. Used as a verb here, which is mostly an American habit; the noun is far more common.
vocabulary.example: Exit the Metro and turn right.

vocabulary.meaning: Change direction to the right. No preposition: “turn right”, never “turn to right”.
vocabulary.example: Exit the Metro and turn right.

vocabulary.meaning: Directly forward, without turning. Answers “which way”, not “how far”.
vocabulary.example: Then walk straight ahead.

vocabulary.meaning: A large shop selling many kinds of goods on several floors. Big enough to be a landmark, which is exactly what it is used for here.
vocabulary.example: My apartment is across from a big department store.
